article_title: Hybrid Instructional Approaches and COVID-19 Infection Trends in a Sample of Pennsylvania School Districts, Fall 2020
citation: Brian Gill, Danielle DeLisle. (2021). Hybrid Instructional Approaches and COVID-19 Infection Trends in a Sample of Pennsylvania School Districts, Fall 2020. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/hybrid-instructional-approaches-and-covid-19-infection-trends-in-a-sample-of-pennsylvania-school-districts-fall-2020
title: Pair hybrid instruction with precautions such as mask-wearing and physical distancing to mitigate in-school virus transmission
description: The report's central design recommendation is that districts can educate students in person while mitigating COVID-19 spread by combining hybrid scheduling with precautions. It asks whether "districts using hybrid approaches (alongside precautions such as mask-wearing and physical distancing) can successfully mitigate in-school virus transmission." The examined districts' experience suggests this combination kept school infection increases no greater than community increases.
requirements: Hybrid instruction must be implemented alongside precautions such as mask-wearing and physical distancing
constraints: Evidence comes from seven examined Pennsylvania districts during fall 2020 and is suggestive rather than experimental
target_learners: K-12 students in school districts operating during the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learning_goals: Maintaining in-person educational access while limiting infectious disease transmission in schools
examples: Mathematica examined seven Pennsylvania school districts using hybrid instruction with precautions and compared their infection trends to local community trends in fall 2020

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Lifelong Learning: Opportunities and Challenges in Adult Education Policy
citation: Theodora, A., & Tselios, N. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Lifelong Learning: Opportunities and Challenges in Adult Education Policy.
title: Hybrid intelligence: human and artificial intelligence complementing one another in adult learning
description: The paper introduces hybrid intelligence as a recent theoretical approach in which "human and artificial intelligence complement one another." In this view AI does not replace human thinking but extends it, supporting decision-making, reflection, and problem-solving. The authors align this with the idea that effective educational systems should combine human judgment with data-driven insights, particularly in complex adult learning contexts.
requirements: Effective educational systems must combine human judgment with data-driven insights rather than delegating decisions wholly to AI.
constraints: The paper presents hybrid intelligence as a theoretical position attributed to recent literature (Cukurova; OECD), not as a tested model.
target_learning_goals: supporting decision-making, reflection, and problem-solving through human-AI complementarity
key_sources: Theodora, A., & Tselios, N. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Lifelong Learning: Opportunities and Challenges in Adult Education Policy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16296

article_title: Confidence Estimation in Automatic Short Answer Grading with LLMs
citation: Longwei Cong, Sonja Hahn, Sebastian Gombert, Leon Camus, Hendrik Drachsler, and Ulf Kroehne. (2026). Confidence Estimation in Automatic Short Answer Grading with LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00200
title: Hybrid confidence framework integrating model-based confidence with dataset-derived aleatoric uncertainty via semantic heterogeneity
description: The framework treats LLM grading unreliability as arising from two sources: epistemic uncertainty, estimated from model-based signals (verbalized, latent, and consistency-based confidence), and aleatoric uncertainty, estimated from the dataset. Aleatoric uncertainty is operationalized by embedding student responses with a sentence-transformer model, clustering them with Ward linkage, and computing normalized Shannon entropy of label distributions within each cluster as a heterogeneity proxy. The signals are fused by a Random Forest classifier with Platt scaling into a calibrated hybrid confidence score. The article states it proposes "a hybrid confidence framework that integrates model-based confidence signals with an explicit estimate of dataset-derived aleatoric uncertainty."
requirements: A calibration subset of labeled student responses to estimate cluster label distributions and learn the classifier's calibration mapping
Human-annotated correctness labels for training the fusion classifier
constraints: Evaluated on a binary correct/incorrect scoring setting with one open-weight model (gpt-oss-20b) and one dataset; the authors state generalizability across models, domains, and annotation schemes remains to be assessed
target_learners: students whose short constructed responses are automatically graded in science assessment
target_learning_goals: accurate and reliable automated scoring of short constructed-response answers to support human-in-the-loop assessment
examples: On the SciEntsBank Test_UD split, responses were embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, clustered with agglomerative hierarchical clustering, and cluster entropies assigned to test responses via nearest centroid
key_sources: Longwei Cong, Sonja Hahn, Sebastian Gombert, Leon Camus, Hendrik Drachsler, and Ulf Kroehne. (2026). Confidence Estimation in Automatic Short Answer Grading with LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00200

article_title: Generative AI offers more, but students revise less: comparing the effects of teacher and AI feedback on student essay revisions
citation: Farrokhnia, M., Latifi, S., Papadopoulos, P. M., Hogenkamp, L., Gijlers, H., Khosravi, H., & Noroozi, O. (2026). Generative AI offers more, but students revise less: comparing the effects of teacher and AI feedback on student essay revisions. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00579-9
title: Use hybrid intelligent feedback systems in which teachers support students in interpreting and applying GenAI feedback
description: The article proposes combining GenAI feedback with teacher support so that teachers help students interpret and apply machine-generated comments. Although CoT-prompted GenAI produced the highest-rated feedback, "this higher feedback quality did not lead to significantly greater improvements in revisions", so the article argues that "students’ engagement with and uptake of feedback play a critical role" and highlights "hybrid intelligent feedback systems in which teachers support students in interpreting and applying GenAI feedback".
requirements: Teachers must be available to help students interpret and apply GenAI feedback during revision
constraints: The article reports that feedback quality alone is insufficient to enhance writing outcomes
target_learners: higher education students writing argumentative essays
target_learning_goals: improving argumentative essay quality through feedback uptake and revision
examples: In the experiment, all three feedback conditions produced comparable revision gains, and feedback quality predicted revisions only in the teacher condition
key_sources: Farrokhnia, M., Latifi, S., Papadopoulos, P. M., Hogenkamp, L., Gijlers, H., Khosravi, H., & Noroozi, O. (2026). Generative AI offers more, but students revise less: comparing the effects of teacher and AI feedback on student essay revisions. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00579-9

article_title: Hypergamigication Through Integrating Game Engines and Learning Management Systems: Ender's Game
citation: Araz Yusubov, Tangiz Alizada, Michael Bechtel. (2026). Hypergamigication Through Integrating Game Engines and Learning Management Systems: Ender's Game. https://github.com/ADA-SITE-SITE4890-2023-Spring/senior-design-project-ay5-gamification-2-0-unity-bb/
title: Hypergamification: bidirectional LMS-game integration where the whole game environment is generated from LMS content
description: Hypergamification is the authors' proposed concept in which a complete game environment, not just isolated game design elements, is generated from LMS learning materials and course structure, and gameplay translates back into course activities. The paper states that "In a bi directional integration model, learners will experience a virtual in -game environment that is generated based on the learning materials and course structure provided by the LMS." It is positioned beyond gamification's points, badges, and leaderboards.
requirements: An LMS exposing course content and activity data through interoperability APIs, and a game engine able to consume and write back that data
constraints: The pilot implements only partial bidirectionality: most tested endpoints were GET retrieval, with CreateMessage() as the only method sending data back to the LMS
target_learners: higher education students using an institutional LMS
target_learning_goals: engagement with course materials, activities, and assessments through a game environment
examples: The demo game renders course portals, announcements, assignments, grades, and weekly material folders as in-game 3D objects drawn from Blackboard data
key_sources: Araz Yusubov, Tangiz Alizada, Michael Bechtel. (2026). Hypergamigication Through Integrating Game Engines and Learning Management Systems: Ender's Game. https://github.com/ADA-SITE-SITE4890-2023-Spring/senior-design-project-ay5-gamification-2-0-unity-bb/

article_title: A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant
citation: Saptarshi Basu, Sandeep Kakar, Ashok Goel. (2026). A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03402
title: Hybrid micro-level personalization framework combining learner-driven preferences with system-driven Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive assessment
description: A framework for personalizing LLM/RAG teaching assistants at the level of individual student questions. It represents learner characteristics through self-assessed metacognitive knowledge and question-level cognitive complexity via Bloom's Taxonomy, plus five Felder-Silverman-derived preferences (abstraction, verbosity, perception, processing, understanding). The article states "The combination of learner characteristics and preferences produces 96 distinct learner profiles" and that "This creates a hybrid framework combining learner-driven adaptability with system-driven adaptivity." It contrasts with prior adaptive systems that adapt content selection or sequencing by instead adapting response form.
requirements: Learner preferences are explicitly selected by students while cognitive demand is inferred by the system via a fine-tuned BERT-based Bloom classifier (0.92 test accuracy)
An engineered prompt encoding all learner attributes must condition the LLM within the existing RAG pipeline and course-specific knowledge base
constraints: Personalization modifies the form and presentation of responses while preserving grounding in retrieved instructional content
Treated as user-selected preferences rather than fixed psychometric classifications
target_learners: online and course-based higher-education students (e.g., KBAI graduate course)
target_learning_goals: tailoring instructional explanations to learner preferences and question cognitive complexity
examples: An example prompt tells the assistant the learner is a beginner, the question is Synthesis-level, and requests a technical, concise, sensory, reflective, global response to the Sheep and Wolves problem
key_sources: Saptarshi Basu, Sandeep Kakar, Ashok Goel. (2026). A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03402

article_title: A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support
citation: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349
title: Hybrid qualitative-plus-center-of-mass model for reasoning about path and support in Camelot Jr.
description: The article presents a hybrid qualitative solver for Camelot Jr. that formalizes the game state symbolically and integrates physics. The agent 'leverages a symbolic paradigm to investigate the game state using common-sense logic, formalizing environmental interactions through qualitative structural affordances', while 'we integrate this symbolic layer with a numerical center-of-mass (COM) stability logic' because the game mechanics involve complex physical equilibria. Qualitative modules describe the grid, blocks, orientations and walkable affordances; the numerical COM logic verifies that block assemblies remain stable under gravitational torque; a graph traversal module checks path connectivity.
requirements: Game states must be translatable into the qualitative grid representation with blocks, towers, Knight and Princess positions
Every placed structure must satisfy the global stability rule under gravitational torque before a path is evaluated
constraints: The model is designed for the Camelot Jr. block-puzzle domain and its specific rules (fixed towers, mandatory use of all inventory blocks, ramp cells that cannot support other blocks)
target_learning_goals: structural stability reasoning
spatial path planning and visualization
examples: The solver places inventory blocks one by one, verifies COM stability of the full assembly, then extracts a walkable path from Knight to Princess via cell affordances
key_sources: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349

article_title: What Students Actually Ask: Demand Structure and Automation Potential in a Hybrid Support System
citation: Gupta, J., Ayinampudi, P., Aditya B.M.V., Hegade, P., Sharma, R., Sharma, S., Meenakshi, V., Iyengar, S.R.S. (2026). What Students Actually Ask: Demand Structure and Automation Potential in a Hybrid Support System. arXiv:2609.38967. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38967
title: Hybrid query-resolution platform routing queries across AI assistant, peer layer, curated FAQ corpus and administrator escalation
description: A deployed support platform for a large online internship programme that routes each raised query across four paths: an AI chatbot answering only from a curated FAQ corpus, a peer layer where any participant may answer, administrator handling, and a scripted facility. The article states that "The platform routes a raised query first to the AI chatbot, which answers only from a curated corpus of verified FAQ entries, a deliberate restriction that prevents unverified procedural guidance". Peer answers pass through administrator acceptance and senior-administrator final approval before release, and the corpus was revised daily so rule or schedule changes were reflected the same day.
requirements: A curated corpus of verified FAQ entries that is revised daily so procedural changes are reflected the same day
Administrator acceptance and senior-administrator approval of peer answers before release to the asker
constraints: The AI assistant answers only from the curated corpus and cannot report an individual participant's current status
The study covers a single programme across nine weeks of onboarding, with volume peaking in week 3 and tapering after, so it describes an onboarding period rather than a steady state
target_learners: Participants in a large-scale online internship programme during staggered-cohort onboarding
target_learning_goals: Resolving operational onboarding queries (eligibility, documentation, scheduling, status of pending submissions) with short turnaround without a dedicated mentor per student
examples: Over nine weeks (2 May to 6 July 2026) the system handled 4,093 queries from 1,434 participants; corpus reuse covered 21.3% of volume from 114 entries, participants self-resolved 12.2%, and 132 participants authored peer answers
key_sources: Gupta, J., Ayinampudi, P., Aditya B.M.V., Hegade, P., Sharma, R., Sharma, S., Meenakshi, V., Iyengar, S.R.S. (2026). What Students Actually Ask: Demand Structure and Automation Potential in a Hybrid Support System. arXiv:2609.38967. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38967

article_title: Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models
citation: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473
title: Pair LLMs with explicit learner-state representations and transition rules for longitudinal simulation
description: For modeling learning trajectories, the article recommends hybrid architectures that pair an LLM with an explicit learner-state representation and a defined transition rule, such as knowledge tracing, proficiency variables, misconception graphs, or cognitive models. It argues that "Longitudinal simulation benefits from explicit learning mechanisms rather than context-window prompting alone", because prompt-only approaches yield abrupt novice-to-expert jumps and unstable competence across turns. This makes trajectories interpretable and calibratable and failures diagnosable.
requirements: An explicit learner-state representation and a defined transition rule paired with the LLM, so that learning trajectories are interpretable and calibratable
constraints: Prompt-only approaches often yield unrealistic dynamics, including abrupt novice-to-expert jumps, unstable competence across turns, and brittle dependence on phrasing
target_learners: Developers of LLM-based simulated students for longitudinal learning simulation
target_learning_goals: Valid modeling of learning trajectories and sensitivity to instructional interventions
examples: The article names knowledge tracing, proficiency variables, misconception graphs, and cognitive models as candidate explicit learner-state representations with defined transition rules
key_sources: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473

article_title: Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning
citation: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808
title: Hybrid layered knowledge base architecture for personalized e-learning built on systems of mapped ontologies, rules, and data-driven techniques
description: The article proposes a conceptual model of a layered, hybrid knowledge base architecture grounded in mathematical logic for intelligent educational systems. It extends the classical four-model ITS architecture by replacing each single ontology with systems of mapped ontologies and adding storage for procedural knowledge as rules, non-crisp knowledge via fuzzy or probabilistic DL extensions, and implicit knowledge via learning analytics and machine learning. The article states it "differs from most other research in this field by proposing systems of mapped ontologies in the place of every single ontology."
requirements: Requires mapped ontologies, rules, and statistics-based technologies to be integrated so that DL-based and transparent rule-based reasoning can support tutoring decisions and learning path generation
constraints: The number of layers and ontologies in every layer cannot be strictly specified; it depends on every specific implementation
target_learners: learners in intelligent educational systems and intelligent tutoring systems across formal education and professional training
target_learning_goals: personalized and adaptive tutoring, learning path generation and recommendation, knowledge tracing
examples: The architecture incorporates the four main models of the typical ontology-based ITS (domain, student, tutoring, user interface) with mapped ontology systems in each
key_sources: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808

article_title: A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching
citation: Danielewicz, Jane and Peter Elbow. (2009). A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching. College Composition and Communication 61(2). https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.14394/23309
title: Hybrid grading: behavior-based grades up to a threshold, quality-based grades above it
description: The article's organizing framework splits the grading scale by what earns the grade: below the threshold (B), the grade rests wholly on observable behaviors and completion; above it, the grade rests wholly on judged quality of writing. As the authors put it, "about behaviors, we take the gloves off; about quality of writing, we give students the power to decide (again, up to the grade of B)." The framework lets teachers maintain high standards of quality while rewarding behaviors that improve writing, and it underlies their claims about feedback, motivation, and grade inflation.
requirements: A base grade available to every student, not dependent on skill or prior training
Base-grade decisions made without regard to judgments of work quality
constraints: Extending the contract to a contract for an A would require dropping those constraints and specifying quality criteria not every student could attain
The authors developed the framework at strong public universities, though they report Shor and colleagues used contracts with working-class students at urban, commuter colleges
target_learning_goals: writing quality
processes such as revision and peer review
examples: Throughout the semester the authors use only three possible grades—not satisfactory for B, satisfactory for B, and better than B—deferring distinctions among higher grades until final portfolios are read
key_sources: Danielewicz, Jane and Peter Elbow. (2009). A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching. College Composition and Communication 61(2). https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.14394/23309

article_title: Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments
citation: Scheiter, K., & Gerjets, P. (2007). Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments. Educational Psychology Review 19, 285–307. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9046-3
title: Use hypermedia for learning in a sensible way, since effectiveness depends on how it is used
description: The review advances the claim "that hypermedia may be effective only if used in a sensible way," positioning sensible use — rather than hypermedia per se — as the condition for effectiveness. This principle follows from the review's analysis of usability problems, moderating learner characteristics, and conceptual and methodological weaknesses in the research base. It is used to derive guidelines for further research on hypermedia learning.
requirements: Design and use of hypermedia must take into account usability problems, learner characteristics, and conceptual foundations identified in the review
constraints: The article states effectiveness "may" occur only under sensible use; it does not specify operational thresholds in the available text
target_learning_goals: Effective learning from learner-controlled hypermedia instruction
examples: The review derives "a couple of guidelines for further research on hypermedia learning" from this claim and its supporting findings
key_sources: Scheiter, K., & Gerjets, P. (2007). Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments. Educational Psychology Review 19, 285–307. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9046-3

article_title: Brain hyper‐connectivity and operation‐specific deficits during arithmetic problem solving in children with developmental dyscalculia
citation: Rosenberg-Lee, M., Ashkenazi, S., Chen, T., Young, C. B., Geary, D. C., & Menon, V. (2014). Brain hyper-connectivity and operation-specific deficits during arithmetic problem solving in children with developmental dyscalculia. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12216
title: Hyper-connectivity account of developmental dyscalculia: inappropriate task modulation and hyper-connectivity, rather than under-engagement and under-connectivity, underlie arithmetic difficulties
description: This framework proposes that developmental dyscalculia arises not from under-activation of the intraparietal sulcus but from aberrant modulation of parietal circuits and excessive connectivity between the IPS and multiple brain systems. The article states that "inappropriate task modulation and hyper-connectivity, rather than under-engagement and under-connectivity, are the neural mechanisms underlying problem solving difficulties in children with DD". It reframes DD as a fundamental difference in parietal organization rather than developmentally delayed maturation, grounded in the study's activation and gPPI findings across addition and subtraction.
requirements: Requires well-characterized DD and TD groups matched on IQ, reading ability and working memory to distinguish DD-specific effects from general ability differences
constraints: Based on cross-sectional neuroimaging of 7–9-year-old children performing timed arithmetic verification tasks; the authors note performance differences between groups partly influence connectivity findings
target_learners: Children with developmental dyscalculia aged 7–9 years
target_learning_goals: Single-digit addition and subtraction arithmetic problem solving
examples: gPPI analysis revealed IPS hyper-connectivity with fronto-parietal and default mode networks in DD children during both operations, contrary to the predicted immature under-connectivity pattern
key_sources: Rosenberg-Lee, M., Ashkenazi, S., Chen, T., Young, C. B., Geary, D. C., & Menon, V. (2014). Brain hyper-connectivity and operation-specific deficits during arithmetic problem solving in children with developmental dyscalculia. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12216

article_title: Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other?
citation: Döhla D and Heim S (2016). Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other? Front. Psychol. 6:2045. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.02045
title: Hybrid multiple-deficit model of dyslexia allowing single or multiple cognitive deficits
description: The review presents Pennington et al. (2012)'s hybrid model, which organizes four cognitive models of dyslexia by whether there is a single deficit and whether a PA deficit is necessary (Table 1: single phonological deficit, single deficit subtypes, phonological core multiple deficit, multiple deficit). The authors conclude "a hybrid model that encompasses all four possibilities of cognitive single- and multiple deﬁcit models (Table 1) best depicts the causesofdyslexia", because nearly all tested dyslexics had at least one marginal cognitive deficit. The review speculates this hybrid model might also explain developmental dysgraphia.
requirements: Allows a single underlying deficit as well as multiple impaired skills, since many cases show more than one impaired function
constraints: The review notes studies of individual profiles of dysgraphia are urgently needed to test the transfer to dysgraphia
target_learners: school-aged children with reading and writing disorders
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of underlying cognitive deficits in reading and writing disorders
examples: Pennington et al. (2012) compared cognitive single-, multiple- and hybrid deficit models and found nearly all tested dyslexics had at least one marginal (11–25th percentile) cognitive deficit
key_sources: Döhla D and Heim S (2016). Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other? Front. Psychol. 6:2045. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.02045

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study
citation: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5
title: Train metacognitive skills in combination with a specific cognitive strategy, then progress to general framing, to support transfer of metacognitive skills
description: The article's hybrid-training design follows the "principle of specific-to-general": metacognitive skills are initially trained with a cognitive strategy on a specific training task, then applied across various cognitive strategies, "finally resulting in a more general framing", ending with a transfer lesson applying metacognitive skills to everyday life situations. Teacher influence is progressively reduced so students independently solve new tasks and apply the acquired strategies. The study's results support this design for fostering near and far transfer of metacognitive skills.
requirements: Training must combine metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluating) with at least one concrete cognitive strategy, include application sequences across varied tasks, and end with a general-framing transfer lesson.
constraints: Even with hybrid training, the level of metacognitive skills use remained low, and one hybrid condition's far-transfer advantage over control was not significant; the authors discuss further means to support transfer.
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
transfer of metacognitive skills to new learning tasks
examples: Each hybrid condition began with basics of learning and cooperative learning, moved to explicit training of metacognitive skills with the cognitive strategy, continued with application training on various experiments or expository texts, and ended with a transfer lesson on everyday situations, with a reflection questionnaire each lesson.
key_sources: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5

article_title: The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy
citation: Nadja Gentner & Tina Seufert. (2020). The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09227-7
title: Hypermedia environment on empirical research methods with six page-linked cognitive and metacognitive prompts
description: A hypermedia learning environment on empirical research methods containing 23 pages, of which six pages (chapters one and two on empirical methods, hypotheses, and propositional logic) were relevant for the learning session. It featured a navigation bar, forward and backward buttons, hyperlinks connecting pages non-linearly, a notepad, and a search function. The experimental group received "A combination of three cognitive and three metacognitive prompts", each linked to a specific relevant page and visible whenever the learner stayed on or revisited that page.
requirements: Learners must plan navigation, organise content, and monitor and evaluate their learning progress, since successful hypermedia learning requires self-regulation and metacognitive skills
constraints: Only the first two of four chapters were relevant and had to be learned in the 40-minute session
target_learning_goals: understanding scientific hypotheses and propositional logic in empirical research methods
examples: Cognitive prompts cued organisation and elaboration (e.g., asking how to organise the structure of the learning contents); metacognitive prompts cued monitoring (e.g., which main points have not been understood)
key_sources: Nadja Gentner & Tina Seufert. (2020). The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09227-7

article_title: Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
citation: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z
title: Hyponymic relationship between metacognition and metadiscourse: metadiscourse as linguistic expression of metacognition
description: The article proposes that metacognition and metadiscourse stand in a hyponymic relationship, with metacognition as superordinate and metadiscourse as hyponym. As the authors state, "metadiscourse is the linguistic expression of metacognition, and metacognition regulates and monitors the cognitive activity through metadiscourse to some extent". The scale development was designed to corroborate this theoretical rationale combining metacognition and metadiscourse with empirical data, extending metacognition to the specific domain of interactive metadiscourse use in L2 writing.
requirements: The framework applies metacognitive regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating) to a specific domain, here interactive metadiscourse use in L2 argumentative writing
constraints: The study focuses only on metacognitive regulation, not metacognitive knowledge or experiences, in the L2 writing context
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse use in argumentative writing
examples: The MRIM scale operationalizes the framework using Wenden's (1998) tripartite model of planning, monitoring, and evaluating applied to interactive metadiscourse
key_sources: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition
citation: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x
title: Hybrid-training approach: metacognitive skills trained in combination with a cognitive strategy to regulate its application
description: Within the hybrid-training approach (Schuster et al., 2020), students learn to use metacognitive skills to regulate the application of a cognitive strategy, learning both the criteria of high-quality strategy application and their use in planning, monitoring, evaluating, and regulating. The article argues that "the repeated and consistent use of the same quality criteria by metacognitive skills support the automatization of metacognitive skill execution," so that metacognitive skills "require less working memory capacity and leave more capacity for direct information processing, that is content knowledge acquisition."
requirements: A series of training tasks requiring repeated and consistent application of a certain cognitive strategy, so the same quality criteria are practiced repeatedly
constraints: Implementation of hybrid metacognitive skill training costs much more effort than the implementation of a non-hybrid training, and pays off only if transfer to different domains is demonstrated
target_learners: fifth-grade students at the end of primary / beginning of secondary school who do not yet possess developed metacognitive skills
target_learning_goals: high-quality application of cognitive learning strategies and content knowledge acquisition

title: Hybrid productive failure with analogical comparison: schema abstraction through comparing contrasting models
description: The article proposes a hybrid learning design that combines productive failure's two phases (Exploration and Generation, then Consolidation and Knowledge Assembly) with analogical comparison scaffolds. complex systems principles such as feedback, emergence, and tipping points
far across domain transfer of structural concepts

article_title: Hypothesis testing governs strategic motor learning
citation: Wei Ding, Anjuli Niyogi, Jordan A. Taylor & Jonathan S. Tsay. (2026). Hypothesis Testing Governs Strategic Motor Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00428-4
title: Hypothesis testing framework of strategic motor learning
description: A process account in which strategic adaptation operates through hypothesis testing: learners generate candidate action–outcome hypotheses about an environmental change, test them against sensory feedback, discard failures, and iteratively refine actions and hypotheses until a solution is abruptly discovered. The proposed formalization comprises 'a hypothesis space and an inference procedure', with discrete spatial transformations (rotations, mirror reflections, translations, gain changes) each carrying a prior belief, actions sampled in proportion to beliefs, and Bayesian-style belief updating favoring more specific hypotheses. Target geometry shapes which hypotheses remain viable, steering both learning speed and the diversity of adopted rules.
requirements: Feedback that lets learners evaluate candidate action–outcome hypotheses against sensory outcomes
constraints: The authors state they are 'not claiming that hypothesis testing provides a superior account across all regimes of motor learning'—state-space/Kalman models describe implicit recalibration and reinforcement learning captures skill acquisition
target_learners: adults learning new sensorimotor mappings (online participants, mean age ~25)
target_learning_goals: discovering effective movement strategies under changed sensorimotor environments
examples: Participants in the visuomotor rotation task explored the workspace to align a 60° rotated cursor to targets without being told the perturbation's nature; the framework treats their sign flips and mirror reversals as hypothesis tests rather than execution failures.

description: The article frames MUD as involving "hypofrontality", a state of insufficient prefrontal neural activation that fails to support cognitive control, leading to heightened salience attribution to drug cues. Within this framework, the better maintenance of prefrontal activation in the Tai Chi group is interpreted as functional recovery — an improved capacity to sustain task-relevant recruitment of prefrontal resources — rather than neural efficiency. The authors add a speculative motor-learning mechanism: Tai Chi's complex movement sequences may recruit fronto-striatal, dopamine-mediated plasticity pathways.

title: Hybrid reinforcement learning / Bayesian inference model of multidimensional learning
description: A computational model combining reinforcement learning with a statistically optimal Bayesian approach to explain choices in multidimensional reward learning. It updates feature values of the chosen stimulus with learning rate η, decays unchosen features with rate ηk, weights dimensions via δ, and balances RL versus Bayesian attention weights via a free parameter alpha, then maps values to choices through a softmax with inverse temperature β. "Prior research indicates that the hybrid reinforcement learning/Bayes model was the model with the best ﬁt in explaining participants' strategies on the same experimental paradigm." The article uses it to derive computational markers distinguishing ADHD and dyslexia learning dynamics.
requirements: Trial-by-trial choice and reward data from each participant; parameters β, η, ηk, δ, α are fit individually by minimizing the negative log likelihood of choices.
constraints: The Bayesian part assumes complete memory of all stimulus-reward observations, an assumption the model itself makes about the learner.
target_learning_goals: Multidimensional reinforcement learning under uncertain dimension relevance
Discovering which stimulus dimension predicts reward
examples: Parameters were fit individually per participant using the R optim package, estimating the joint likelihood of all choices in each task separately.

description: The article proposes that argument diagramming works through two mechanisms: the spatial structure of diagrams makes some argument aspects salient (relevance of citations, presence or absence of opposition), while the detailed textual fields within diagram components make other aspects salient (such as validity, which varied across frameworks). Integration of team-based learning and simulation-based learning in clinical education of infant feeding and swallowing assessment and management of speech-language pathology students: a retrospective pre-post intervention study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07721-7
title: Hybrid TBL-SBL pedagogical paradigm for complex clinical education
description: The article proposes an integrated pedagogy that sequences team-based learning's knowledge-assurance steps (pre-class preparation, IRAT, TRAT, immediate feedback) with simulation-based learning's phases (pre-briefing, scenario, debriefing). The authors state its "primary contribution is the creation of an innovative hybrid pedagogical paradigm" for enhancing knowledge and confidence in infant dysphagia care, arguing TBL characteristics address shortcomings of SBL identified by Bae et al. at the pre-briefing, scenario and debriefing stages.
requirements: Requires TBL components (micromodule, IRAT, TRAT, feedback) preceding the simulation scenario and a facilitator-led debriefing at closing
constraints: The study implemented a modified integration rather than a 'pure' integration of the two frameworks
Evidence comes from a single-group pre-post design without a control group
target_learning_goals: assessment and management of infant feeding and swallowing disorders
collaborative clinical reasoning and shared decision-making
examples: A 4-hour paediatric feeding clinic combining a 2-hour simulated skills training session, a 12-minute micromodule with IRAT, and a 2-hour case simulation with TRAT
key_sources: Kwan Connie Ching-Yin, Weir Kelly Ann, Fong Raymond, Pereira Valerie Jane, Law Thomas. (2025). Integration of team-based learning and simulation-based learning in clinical education of infant feeding and swallowing assessment and management of speech-language pathology students: a retrospective pre-post intervention study. article_title: Evaluating AI-generated examination papers in periodontology: a comparative study with human-designed counterparts.
citation: Ma Xiang, Pan Wei, Yu Xiao-ning. (2025). Evaluating AI-generated examination papers in periodontology: a comparative study with human-designed counterparts. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07706-6
title: Hybrid AI-human collaborative generation framework for examination design
description: The article proposes a hybrid "AI-human collaborative generation" framework that combines automated item generation with human expert calibration, integrating medical knowledge graphs for contextual optimization of items. It is motivated by the finding that AI papers achieved breadth and efficiency but lacked clinical contextualization and discrimination, so automation is balanced "with assessment precision". The framework positions AI as augmentation of, not replacement for, human expertise in assessment design.
requirements: AI pre-screening of generated items followed by expert refinement
knowledge-graph-enhanced distractor complexity to model clinical reasoning
constraints: GPT-4 used in the study was not specifically fine-tuned for medical item construction, resulting in insufficient item discrimination
the framework is proposed, not empirically tested, in this study
target_learning_goals: assessment of periodontology knowledge, including clinical reasoning and procedural integration
examples: the study generated the AI paper via GPT-4 with expert-crafted prompts and had one periodontology teacher review the content to ensure no incorrect questions
key_sources: Ma Xiang, Pan Wei, Yu Xiao-ning. (2025). Evaluating AI-generated examination papers in periodontology: a comparative study with human-designed counterparts. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07706-6

article_title: Implementation of hybrid simulation training to promote collective and self-efficacy in medical students: a two-pronged approach.
citation: Tam, C. Y. W., Dizon, J. I. W. T., Sin, S. W. C., Tang, G. K. Y., Lai, V. Y. W., Wong, Y. Y., Ganotice, F. A., & Yeung, N. P. (2025). Implementation of hybrid simulation training to promote collective and self-efficacy in medical students: a two-pronged approach. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2025.2527362
title: Hybrid SBT setup: BodyInteract virtual patient simulator paired with a basic CPR manikin in facilitated team-based acute-care scenarios
description: The hybrid SBT environment combines "a simple bedside environment with one basic CPR manikin and an interactive display monitor" projecting the BodyInteract VPS software. A teaching clinician leads objectives and debriefs while a simulation facilitator mirrors physical exams performed on the manikin to the VPS and enters management plans, so student actions produce real-time feedback as the virtual patient improves or deteriorates. Each 10-student session splits into five active participants and five observing students who chart actions, across two scenarios (unconscious patient with intracranial haemorrhage; sepsis secondary to pneumonia).
requirements: Two staff per session: a teaching clinician and a simulation facilitator to bridge manikin and VPS
Staff receive brief training on the VPS and scenarios, supplemented by a tutor guide
constraints: Scenarios limited to cases available within the BodyInteract software
target_learners: fifth-year undergraduate medical students in ICU clerkships
target_learning_goals: systematic ABCDE assessment of unstable patients
septic shock identification and sepsis-1-hour bundle resuscitation
basic airway management
team-based acute-care management
examples: Two roughly 10-minute debriefs reinforced key learning objectives; scenarios were developed based on Kolb's experiential learning theory.

article_title: Enhancing medical assessment strategies: a comparative study between structured, traditional and hybrid viva-voce assessment.
citation: Rasalkar Kavita, Tripathy Sunita, Sinha Sulekha, Mukherjee Bikramaditya, Takkella Nagamma, Dadel Elvis Vishal, Sundriyal Monit, Prasad Swetanka. (2025). Enhancing medical assessment strategies: a comparative study between structured, traditional and hybrid viva-voce assessment. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07428-9
title: Hybrid viva-voce assessment method combining structured and traditional formats
description: The hybrid method sums the marks a student earns in a structured viva and a traditional viva conducted by the same examiner. The article describes it as an approach that "combines the structured evaluation of a standardized viva with the flexibility of the traditional method", intending to overcome the disadvantages of both individual methods. It emerged as the students' preferred format and showed the highest inter-examiner consistency in the study.
requirements: Both a prepared structured viva card set and an unstructured traditional questioning session per examiner
Sequential 5-minute sessions with each examiner for each student
constraints: The article cautions the observed statistical significance may have been influenced by the larger sample size rather than a true advantage of the method
Single-centre, single-subject context limits generalizability
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive and consistent evaluation of Biochemistry knowledge and clinical reasoning
examples: Hybrid scores were obtained by summing each student's structured and traditional viva marks given by the same examiner.

article_title: Hybrid BOPPPS model in radiology education: a case study of pediatric undergraduates.
citation: Cheng Wei-Qin, He Ling, Cai Jin-Hua, Fan Xiao. (2025). Hybrid BOPPPS model in radiology education: a case study of pediatric undergraduates. BMC Medical Education, 25. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07279-4
title: Online-offline hybrid BOPPPS radiology curriculum with pre-class online nodes and in-class participatory learning
description: A 40-lesson radiology curriculum (16 classroom, 13 online, 11 practice lessons of 40 min each) for the BOPPPS group. Pre-class videos of 10-30 minutes with typical radiological images were watched on the university online platform and "will be documented as a learning node"; teaching assistants uploaded pre-learning assessment one month prior and preview questions one week before each class. After class, homework was posted online and students used a case presentation video library and an online simulation platform for self-learning and revision.
requirements: Teaching assistants to collect and grade pre-learning assessments and send results to instructors before class; an online education platform and teaching software for assessments
constraints: The hybrid model "poses greater demands on teachers to efficiently instruct within the constraints of classroom time"
target_learning_goals: radiological image interpretation and diagnostic reasoning
examples: Three single-choice pre-assessment questions distributed via teaching assistant software during class to tailor upcoming lectures; practice sessions on image interpretation led by two experienced teaching assistants
key_sources: Cheng Wei-Qin, He Ling, Cai Jin-Hua, Fan Xiao. (2025). Hybrid BOPPPS model in radiology education: a case study of pediatric undergraduates. BMC Medical Education, 25. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07279-4

article_title: Hybrid BOPPPS model in radiology education: a case study of pediatric undergraduates.
citation: Cheng Wei-Qin, He Ling, Cai Jin-Hua, Fan Xiao. (2025). Hybrid BOPPPS model in radiology education: a case study of pediatric undergraduates. BMC Medical Education, 25. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07279-4
title: Use structured six-step BOPPPS within a hybrid online-offline model to improve radiology outcomes for undergraduates
description: The article recommends the hybrid BOPPPS model as an effective radiology teaching method for five-year pediatric undergraduates, concluding it "is deserving of recommendation". It structures each lesson around bridge-in, objectives, pre-assessment, participatory learning, post-assessment and summary, supported by pre-class online learning nodes and post-class online resources, so that teaching objectives, instruction and assessment remain constructively aligned.
requirements: Online platforms and teaching software for pre-class materials, learning nodes and in-class assessments; teaching assistants to manage assessment collection and questionnaires
constraints: Cross-academic-year cohort comparisons may introduce temporal confounders; modest absolute gains may reflect Hawthorne effect; long-term outcomes unverified; in-house questionnaire validity may be context-specific
target_learning_goals: imaging interpretation, diagnostic reasoning, course engagement and comprehensive radiology grades
examples: The 2019 cohort received the hybrid BOPPPS curriculum across 40 lessons and outperformed the 2018 LBL cohort on all grade measures without increased study pressure

article_title: Classroom teaching versus online teaching in physiology practical course - does this lead to different examination results?
citation: Dreyer Tom, Papadopoulos Symeon, Wiesner Rudolf, Karay Yassin. (2025). Classroom teaching versus online teaching in physiology practical course – does this lead to different examination results? GMS Journal for Medical Education, 42(1), Doc8. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2025-42/zma001732.shtml
title: Prefer hybrid teaching that combines the advantages of face-to-face and online formats for physiology practical courses
description: The article recommends that, given the measured advantage of face-to-face teaching alongside the flexibility benefits of online teaching, the ideal format is "a hybrid solution that combines the advantages of both formats". It positions hybrid delivery as a way to retain the interaction and hands-on experimentation of presence teaching while preserving the location and time flexibility online delivery offers students. The recommendation follows directly from the study's comparison of exam outcomes between formats.
requirements: Course teams must be able to offer both face-to-face and online (video-conference) delivery of practical classes, as the Cologne institute did via Zoom with live demonstrations and licensed simulation programs.
constraints: The article notes effectiveness "depends heavily on the type of course, but also on the lecturers themselves", and the study is limited to Cologne.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in preclinical physiology courses
target_learning_goals: Physiology practical course knowledge assessed by written examination
examples: The Cologne physiology course ran 15 practical topics in alternating face-to-face and online cohorts, with lectures online for everyone and recordings on the ILIAS e-learning system.

article_title: Evaluation of a hybrid model of a Physician Associate Studies programme: students, teachers, and examiner perspectives.
citation: Joyce P, Cunningham M, Alexander L. (2025). Evaluation of a hybrid model of a Physician Associate Studies programme: students, teachers, and examiner perspectives. Irish Journal of Medical Science 194(2):431-438. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11845-025-03918-3
title: Hybrid model structure: synchronous online didactic teaching with twice-monthly on-campus anatomy, clinical skills, and integration days
description: The programme's hybrid model combines online synchronous instruction with periodic in-person immersion: students "take all their lectures and small group teaching online, coming to campus twice a month for anatomy and clinical teaching". The design aimed to widen access to learners outside Dublin, support mature learners and those from geographically disparate regions, and address workforce shortages in remote areas, with peer-to-peer meetings and faculty advisors layered on to support integration.
requirements: Additional classroom cameras and microphones, timetabling adjusted for twice-monthly campus days, and reliable broadband for students, which is uneven in parts of Ireland
constraints: Internet challenges (adequate broadband coverage) in some parts of Ireland were acknowledged as a barrier to effective remote educational experiences
target_learners: graduate-entry health professions students, including mature learners and those living outside the programme's home city
target_learning_goals: physician associate didactic and clinical competencies delivered across online and in-person modes
examples: The pilot January 2023 intake had six hybrid and eight on-campus students; the January 2024 cohort grew to 16 hybrid and 14 on-campus after HSE tuition funding.

citation: Ali Sana, McMillan Kim, Kelly Freya. (2025). Improving Palliative Care Knowledge of nurses caring for heart failure patients. BMC Palliative Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12904-025-01669-7
title: Hybrid and asynchronous multi-modal delivery of short case-based education sessions for busy clinical staff
description: The intervention delivered 40-minute sessions combining a 20-minute didactic presentation, 10 minutes of case scenario videos, and 10 minutes of discussion, with in-person, virtual, and asynchronous options. The article states "Hybrid learning combines face-to-face and virtual learning and is an effective method in nursing education to enhance knowledge, problem-solving abilities, and learning satisfaction". Case scenario videos on GOC/ACP communication were incorporated to bridge the theory-practice gap, and recorded asynchronous sessions were made available online for four weeks to promote flexible, self-directed learning.
requirements: Sessions designed around identified learning needs and staff-preferred times
Educational materials kept accessible to encourage continuous knowledge use
constraints: Despite flexible modalities, participation remained low; the article notes the increase from asynchronous sessions "was not substantial"
target_learners: Experienced inpatient nurses in tertiary cardiac care
target_learning_goals: Palliative care symptom management
ACP/GOC communication skills
examples: A second virtual session was organized after the first week drew no in-person participation; sessions were recorded for asynchronous viewing after stakeholder feedback

article_title: Design and Development of an Integrated Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Training System for Difficult Airway Management.
citation: Jain Saurabh, Dripta Barua Chowdhury Bijoy, Mosier Jarrod M., Subbian Vignesh, Hughes Kate, Son Young-Jun. (2025). Design and Development of an Integrated Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Training System for Difficult Airway Management. IEEE Journal of Translational Engineering in Health and Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1109/JTEHM.2025.3529748
title: Integrated hybrid VR-based training system for difficult airway management
description: A mixed-reality intubation simulator combining a physical environment (3D-printed manikin, sensor-instrumented laryngoscope and endotracheal tube) with a virtual emergency room built in Unity 3D. As the article states, "The proposed system consists of two interconnected components: the physical environment and the virtual environment", with one-to-one mapping, real-time haptic feedback, pressure-driven soft-tissue deformation, and a multi-modal sensing framework capturing performance and biometric data for training and research.
requirements: Photorealistic patient environment rendering with visual, auditory and haptic feedback
Real-time tracking of procedural tools and streaming of pressure distribution into the simulation
Accurate calibration of virtual anatomical structures with the physical manikin
constraints: Lacks integrated evaluation tools for automated performance assessment, a limitation the authors state in the conclusion
target_learning_goals: endotracheal intubation procedural skill
decision-making under physiologically difficult airway scenarios
stress inoculation in high-stakes airway management
examples: Validation studies at a university medical education center with seven expert clinicians using the AirSim Advance X manikin integrated into the system

article_title: Physiotherapy students' academic performance and satisfaction after following a chest physiotherapy course in hybrid mode: a case-control study.
citation: Bellini Raffaella, Rossettini Giacomo, Letafatkar Amir, Dell’Isola Andrea, Battista Simone. (2024). Physiotherapy students’ academic performance and satisfaction after following a chest physiotherapy course in hybrid mode: a case-control study. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-76051-3
title: Use hybrid teaching for theoretical lectures, but not as a substitute for face-to-face teaching of hands-on skills
description: The article recommends hybrid classes as "a helpful alternative for theoretical lectures that do not involve acquiring manual skills", since students can choose to attend in person and remote attendance reduces travel and accommodation costs. Its own data support this split: remote attendance disadvantaged practical skills (effect size 2.05) but showed no conclusive disadvantage for theoretical knowledge. The authors state the conclusion "does not extend to teaching hands-on activities".
requirements: A hybrid format with simultaneous in-person and video-conferenced attendance, and assessment tools separating theoretical knowledge from practical skills
constraints: The conclusion does not extend to teaching hands-on activities; the study had short-term follow-up only and no students practised the techniques before evaluation
target_learners: undergraduate physiotherapy students in their final year
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge of airway clearance techniques and devices
practical skills in chest physiotherapy
examples: Students were randomly divided so half attended the six-hour seminar in person and half remotely; face-to-face students outperformed remote students on the practical checklist but not conclusively on the quiz

Physiotherapy students’ academic performance and satisfaction after following a chest physiotherapy course in hybrid mode: a case-control study. article_title: Examiner workload comparison: three structured oral examination formats for the European diploma in anaesthesiology and intensive care.
citation: Dziadzko Mikhail, Varvinskiy Andrey, Di Loreto Rodolphe, Scipioni Hugues, Ateleanu Bazil, Klimek Markus, Berger-Estilita Joana. (2024). Examiner workload comparison: three structured oral examination formats for the European diploma in anaesthesiology and intensive care. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2364990
title: Prefer a hybrid examination mode combining physical examiner presence with remote candidates to balance workload, efficiency and accessibility
description: The article proposes the hybrid format — physical presence of examiner pairs with remote online participation of candidates — as a way of conducting examinations that reduces perceived examiner workload while preserving integrity. It reports that "the hybrid examination mode... was associated with a reduction in perceived workload" and argues the approach "could offer a more balanced and efficient way of conducting examinations while maintaining their integrity and effectiveness", with potential cost savings and improved accessibility for candidates.
requirements: Examination infrastructure supporting both a physical plenary/examiner venue and remote candidate participation, with an examination office organising interactions between examiners and candidates
constraints: The workload reduction was statistically significant but relatively small, less than 30%; the article states this potential rather than a demonstrated advantage for grading quality
target_learners: postgraduate medical examination candidates and examiner pairs in high-stakes oral assessment
target_learning_goals: standardised evaluation of professional knowledge with reduced examiner burden and improved candidate accessibility
examples: In the 2023 EDAIC Part 2 cycle, hybrid examinations had examiner pairs physically present with candidates participating remotely, and only 2 of 73 hybrid measurements reached very high workload versus 13 of 104 online

article_title: EndoTrainer: a novel hybrid training platform for endoscopic surgery.
citation: Hernansanz A, Rovira R, Basomba J, Comas R, Casals A. (2023). EndoTrainer: a novel hybrid training platform for endoscopic surgery. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-023-02837-x
title: Hybrid physical-virtual training platforms: combining physical realism with virtual measurement, evaluation and AR feedback
description: The article articulates a hybrid approach to surgical skills training that merges the two dominant platform types. Physical platforms give realistic tools, haptics and environment interaction but no automatic assessment; virtual simulators give objective evaluation and varied scenarios but lack realism and remain expensive. Hybrid platforms are described as "based on a physical device that reproduces the anatomical cavity, allows the use of real surgical tools and presents the capability of measuring and evaluating in real time the execution of the exercises", adding augmented reality as a virtual mentor. EndoTrainer is the article's instantiation of this framework.
requirements: Real-time data fusion from tool tracking, computer vision and workspace sensors to link the physical and virtual sides
Measurement and evaluation capacities, which the article calls "the link between the physical and virtual platforms"
constraints: Orthopaedic surgery, with rigid anatomical structures, facilitates implementation of this type of simulator; natural-orifice applications are less developed
Only a very few hybrid platforms for minimally invasive surgery have been validated
target_learners: Surgical trainees learning minimally invasive and natural-orifice endoscopic procedures
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor surgical skills
Camera navigation and instrument handling
Objective assessment of skill evolution
examples: EndoTrainer combines silicon-based anatomical cavities with Tool Tracker Arm kinematics and AR-generated critical situations
Related validated hybrid systems cited: LTS3e laparoscopic simulator, PRoMIS by Haptica, VirtaMed simulators with realistic physical setup
key_sources: Hernansanz A, Rovira R, Basomba J, Comas R, Casals A. (2023). EndoTrainer: a novel hybrid training platform for endoscopic surgery. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-023-02837-x

article_title: Simulation-based training in ear, nose and throat skills and emergencies.
citation: MK Goutham, Saldanha Marina, Bhat Vadisha S., A Rajeshwary, Vincent Mark Jittu, Ravikumar Aishwarya. (2023). Simulation-based training in ear, nose and throat skills and emergencies. Brazilian Journal of Otorhinolaryngology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjorl.2022.01.001
title: Hybrid lecture-plus-simulation training model with objective standardized assessment for ENT emergencies
description: The article's training model combines a 1-hour lecture-based teaching program with PowerPoint, video demonstration and scenario-specific hands-on mannequin training, followed by objective checklist-based assessment in a simulated environment. The authors state that "Simulation training followed by objective assessment improves retention and application" and that the simulation-based hybrid approach improves cognitive, psychomotor skills and confidence. Assessment used a validated questionnaire and expert-validated checklists with three assessors to minimize bias.
requirements: A validated questionnaire and checklist for the trained scenarios
Hands-on simulation training on mannequins for the assigned scenario
Assessment in a simulated environment under supervision to standardize scoring
constraints: Assessment was completed within the 15-day posting window; repeat assessment after three months was not possible because participants had postings in other departments
Participants' prior exposure to scenarios during postings could have biased assessment
target_learners: Medical interns in rotatory ENT postings with no prior exposure to ENT emergencies
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, confidence and psychomotor skills in managing ENT emergencies and procedures (tracheostomy care, epistaxis management, nasogastric tube insertion)
examples: Interns in batches of 5-6 received pre-test, 1-hour lecture on three scenarios, hands-on mannequin training on their assigned scenario only, and day-15 checklist-scored simulation assessment of all three scenarios

article_title: A novel algorithm-driven hybrid simulation learning method to improve acquisition of endotracheal intubation skills: a randomized controlled study.
citation: Mankute A, Juozapaviciene L, Stucinskas J, Dambrauskas Z, Dobozinskas P, Sinz E, Rodgers DL, Giedraitis M, Vaitkaitis D. (2022). A novel algorithm-driven hybrid simulation learning method to improve acquisition of endotracheal intubation skills: a randomized controlled study. BMC Anesthesiology 22:42. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12871-021-01557-6
title: HybridLab algorithm-driven hybrid simulation learning method
description: The HybridLab method at the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences combines distance learning on an e-learning platform with small-group peer-to-peer simulation training under remote instructor supervision. The article states the method "offers a well-structured and standardized learning pathway, which encompasses studies on an e-learning platform, peer-to-peer hands-on training sessions in the skill lab or simulation classes using carefully elaborated learning algorithms, direct feedback by peers, and assessment by a remotely working instructor". Learners in groups of three use tablets with proprietary educational software, electronic scenarios, checklists and learning algorithms, with 24/7 lab access and video-recorded sessions reviewed remotely by teachers who give feedback by email.
requirements: Learners must pass an online test of 10 questions with a perfect score before starting practical training

Training labs with installed cameras and hand-held tablets containing proprietary educational software, electronic scenarios and checklists are needed so training can proceed without a technician or instructor
constraints: The method was studied with 5th-year medical students and first-year Emergency Medicine and Anesthesiology residents learning endotracheal intubation
target_learners: first-year residents in Emergency Medicine and Anesthesiology
target_learning_goals: endotracheal intubation procedural skill
safe airway management principles
peer feedback and assessment skills
examples: In the study, the hybrid group studied theory, lectures, videos and algorithms on a virtual learning environment, then trained peer-to-peer in groups of three with the same manikin and equipment as the conventional group, plus tablet-based algorithms and checklists.

article_title: Involving hybrid professionals in top management decision-making: How managerial training can make the difference.
citation: Giacomelli G, Ferré F, Furlan M, Nuti S. (2019). Involving hybrid professionals in top management decision-making: How managerial training can make the difference. Health Services Management Research, 32(4), 168–179. https://doi.org/10.1177/0951484819844778
title: Hybrid professionals and the two-fold clinical-managerial role
description: Hybrid professionals hold a role that is simultaneously clinical and managerial. As the article states, "Hybrid professionals have a two-fold – professional and managerial – role, which requires appropriate management skills". In healthcare, clinical directors must combine high-level clinical competencies with organizational and relational skills to lead their departments and report to top management, bridging a clinical culture based on collegial authority and personal responsibility with a managerial culture based on hierarchical authority and shared responsibility. Managerial training is proposed as a mechanism supporting engagement with managerialism.
requirements: Appropriate management skills acquired through managerial training programs to complement clinical competencies
constraints: The role depends on the institutional context; a cross-country study cited in the article shows doctors' involvement in top management decision-making is often consultative rather than decisional
target_learners: Clinicians with management roles, such as clinical directors and heads of department
target_learning_goals: Managerial competencies including performance management, budgeting, goal setting and strategic planning
Engagement with managerialism and upward influence on top management decision-making
examples: Italian law requires heads of department to complete a minimum of 100 certified hours of managerial training before taking charge of their role

title: Hypothesis-driven, case-based auscultation lab: students anticipate findings before hearing simulated heart sounds
description: The lab presents students with unknown clinical vignettes and, before playing the associated heart sounds on the simulator, asks them which sounds they would anticipate, then follows with probing questions on location, diagnoses, and pathophysiology. The article states that "the HDPE approach has been shown to increase learner retention and understanding of the significance of physical findings." The session pairs group case work with direct individual auscultation practice on the manikin.
requirements: Faculty facilitators with a background in cardiac auscultation skills
An auscultation simulator capable of producing normal and pathologic heart sounds
Vignettes and probing questions prepared in advance, with a facilitator manual
constraints: In a large-group adaptation, students would not have the opportunity to auscultate the manikin directly
target_learning_goals: identify and discriminate between normal and pathologic heart sounds
interpret heart sounds in the context of a patient scenario
examples: Students were presented with eight unknown clinical scenarios; facilitators asked students to anticipate heart sounds before playing them on the simulator

title: Hygiene competence as a multidimensional personal disposition of knowledge, attitudes, and behavioral routines
description: The article defines hygiene competence as a set of personal dispositions applied in typical professional situations, encompassing specialized knowledge, specific attitudes, and practical skills. It states that clinical staff who are competent "have various personal resources, i.e. characteristics and dispositions, which are the basis for successful performance in professional situations." The model is offered as a theoretically grounded conception where the literature previously used the term without differentiation.
requirements: A theoretical model capturing the complex and multidimensional nature of the ability to work hygienically, as the article argues such a model is helpful and necessary
constraints: The article notes the theoretical relation to current debates on competence is not yet completely worked out in the present text
target_learners: medical, nursing, and therapeutic clinical staff
target_learning_goals: working hygienically correctly across diverse clinical tasks and situations
examples: The model distinguishes knowledge (microbiology, guidelines), attitudes (self-efficacy, self-regulation), and skills (hand disinfection, sterile catheter placement) as three facets merging in clinical professional behavior

title: Contextual model classifying influences on hygienic clinical behavior as enablers, promoters, and barriers
description: Alongside the competence model, the article proposes a contextual model classifying influence factors on hygienic clinical behavior. Enablers are structural conditions (personnel, materials, guidelines) that are "necessary but not sufficient conditions"; promoters include training, feedback, and role models; barriers include high workload, time pressure, and lacking disinfection fixtures. The article states that "observing the clinical behavior of individuals outside of the context in which it occurs makes little sense."
requirements: Institutional responsibility for providing enabler factors such as sufficient personnel, disinfectant dispensers, and clothing guidelines
constraints: Role models appear among promoters when present and among barriers when absent, since positive role models seem to be rather lacking currently
target_learners: clinical staff in hospitals and practices
target_learning_goals: adherence to hygiene standards in daily clinical routine
examples: Barriers listed include high workload, too few personnel, high time pressure, impractically placed sinks, and high-risk activities in the OR, anesthesia theater, emergency room, or ICU

title: Hygie: a web-based serious game for continuing medical education of general practitioners built from evidence-based journal articles
description: Hygie is a prototype HTML5 video game in which the player is a GP treating patients across the 5 most frequent reasons for consultation in France. transfer of knowledge to practice

article_title: Association between emotional intelligence and academic success among undergraduates: A cross-sectional study in KUST, Pakistan.
citation: Suleman Qaiser, Hussain Ishtiaq, Syed Makhdoom Ali, Parveen Rashida, Lodhi Ishrat Siddiqa, Mahmood Ziarab. (2019). title: Emotional Intelligence Scale (EIS) by Hyde, Pethe, and Dhar: 34-item, ten-subdimension instrument used in Urdu translation
description: The Emotional Intelligence Scale (EIS) developed by Hyde, Pethe, and Dhar is a 34-item, five-point Likert instrument measuring ten subdimensions: self-awareness, emotional stability, empathy, managing relations, integrity, self-motivation, commitment, self-development, value orientation, and altruistic behaviour. The article reports the scale's split-half reliability coefficient and content validity as 0.88 and 0.93 respectively, and used an Urdu translation pilot-tested with 30 undergraduates. Test-retest reliability in this study showed a strong positive correlation (r = 0.995) for overall emotional intelligence.
requirements: Proper formal permission was sought from the authors of the EIS before use.
constraints: The scale was validated on Indian executives, so the authors judged it necessary to confirm its validity and reliability in the Pakistani perspective and translated it into Urdu.
target_learning_goals: measuring emotional intelligence as a correlate of academic success
examples: The instrument was pilot tested through 30 undergraduate students selected randomly from different departments of KUST, and its test-retest reliability was checked over a fifteen-day interval.

article_title: Training medical students to manage difficult circumstances- a curriculum for resilience and resourcefulness?
citation: Wright Barry; Richmond Mynett Joseph. (2019). Training medical students to manage difficult circumstances- a curriculum for resilience and resourcefulness? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1712-x
title: The HYMS CARE criteria: a four-theme taxonomy of 31 resilience-building factors for curriculum evaluation
description: The HYMS CARE criteria (HCC) are an itemised inventory of factors believed to influence resilience and resourcefulness among medical students, organised in three levels: "31 individual elements, 10 groups of elements and 4 overall themes". The four themes are internal resources, lifestyle factors, external resources (self-mediated) and external resources (agent-mediated), isolating forces from the individual's impact on their environment to the environment's impact on the individual. The acronym stands for Compassion to self and others, Adaptability, Resourcefulness and Emotional wellbeing. The authors state it is "not intended as a definitive exposition of resilience, rather a tool that can be used to navigate areas of interest and assess current curricula".
requirements: An expert group of educators, clinicians and students to agree the principles on which the curriculum is assessed
Course documents outlining content that is planned, explicit, universal and quantifiable
constraints: Not a definitive exposition of resilience; a navigation and assessment tool
Only constant elements of variable components such as clinical placements are assessable
target_learning_goals: Resilience and resourcefulness
Coping with stressors and difficult circumstances
